WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Shortly before President Obama embarks on a trip to the Middle East, a new national poll suggests that only one in five Americans holds a favorable view of Muslim countries.

That figure stands in contrast to the 46 percent of respondents in a CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey who say they hold an unfavorable opinion of Muslim countries—an increase of 5 percentage points from 2002, when 41 percent expressed such a view. Meanwhile, three in 10 report a neutral opinion of Muslim countries.

The poll also indicates that most Americans suspect people in Muslim countries do not think highly of the United States. Nearly eight in 10 respondents believe that people in Muslim countries hold an unfavorable opinion of the United States, while 14 percent say Muslims maintain a favorable view.

Yet the poll reveals that Americans appear divided on whether such negative opinions among Muslims are of consequence. Fifty-three percent of those surveyed say they believe Muslim views of the United States matter greatly or moderately, whereas 47 percent contend that Muslim opinions of the United States matter little or not at all.

The poll's release comes just hours before the president departs for Saudi Arabia to meet with King Abdullah. Following his visit to Saudi Arabia, Obama will travel to Egypt, where he is scheduled to deliver a long-awaited address Thursday on relations between the United States and the Muslim world.

At a town hall meeting in Turkey earlier this year, the president declared that "the United States is not, and will never be, at war with Islam." Many Americans appear to share this sentiment: Sixty-two percent of those surveyed say they do not believe the United States is at war with the Muslim world, while 36 percent maintain that the country is at war with Muslim nations. These figures have remained steady since CNN's 2002 poll. However, the poll suggests that six out of 10 respondents believe the Muslim world considers itself at war with the United States.

"The feeling seems to be mutual. We distrust Muslims. They distrust Americans. Views of Americans have not changed very much over the past seven years. There are some indications that Muslims' views of Americans have improved a bit since Barack Obama took office, but they are still not positive," said Bill Schneider, CNN senior political analyst.

The CNN/Opinion Research poll was conducted May 14-17, surveying 1,010 adult Americans by telephone. The survey carries a sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

A recent poll conducted by CNN and the Opinion Research Corporation has revealed significant insights into how Americans perceive Muslim countries and their relationship with the United States.

According to the survey, only one in five Americans holds a favorable view of Muslim countries, while nearly half—46 percent—expressed an unfavorable opinion. These figures point to a considerable degree of skepticism among the American public regarding Muslim-majority nations.

Notably, this unfavorable sentiment has grown over time. The 46 percent figure represents a 5-percentage-point increase since 2002, when the unfavorable rating stood at 41 percent. This upward trend suggests that negative perceptions have deepened over the intervening years.

As President Obama prepared to embark on his Middle East trip and deliver a landmark speech aimed at improving relations between the United States and the Muslim world, a newly released CNN/Opinion Research Corporation poll offered a revealing snapshot of American public opinion. The survey examined how Americans view Muslim countries and, just as importantly, how they believe Muslims around the world perceive the United States.

The findings paint a picture of persistent skepticism and mutual distrust. According to the poll, only about one in five Americans—roughly 20 percent—reported holding a favorable view of Muslim countries. By contrast, 46 percent expressed an unfavorable opinion, a figure that represents a notable increase from levels recorded in 2002. This upward shift in negative sentiment suggests that, despite the passage of years, American attitudes toward the Muslim world have grown more, rather than less, guarded.

The survey also probed Americans' beliefs about how they are perceived abroad. Here, the results were striking: nearly 80 percent of respondents believed that Muslims around the world hold an unfavorable view of the United States. This widespread perception of being disliked underscores the sense of estrangement that the President's trip and speech sought to address.

Yet the poll was not entirely defined by division. Despite these unfavorable impressions, most Americans firmly rejected the notion that the United States is at war with the Muslim world as a whole. This distinction indicates that while many Americans harbor reservations about Muslim countries, they do not view the relationship as one of outright conflict or irreconcilable hostility.

Taken together, the poll's findings provided important context for President Obama's diplomatic efforts. His outreach came at a moment when American public opinion reflected both wariness toward Muslim nations and an awareness of the strained perceptions that existed on both sides—challenges the administration hoped its engagement would help to overcome.

# New Poll Reveals Complex American Attitudes Toward Muslim World Ahead of Obama's Egypt Speech

**Washington (CNN)** — As President Obama prepares to depart for the Middle East and deliver a highly anticipated address to the Muslim world from Cairo, a new poll released Tuesday reveals that Americans hold nuanced and often conflicting views about Muslim-majority nations and Islam more broadly.

The survey, conducted over the past week, comes at a pivotal moment for the administration, which has sought to reset relations with Muslim countries after years of tension during the previous administration's war on terror.

## Divided Opinions

According to the poll, Americans remain split on their overall perception of Muslim nations. Roughly 46 percent of respondents said they held favorable views toward predominantly Muslim countries, while a comparable share expressed unfavorable opinions. The findings underscore the challenge Obama faces as he attempts to bridge divides both abroad and at home.

"These numbers reflect a country still grappling with the aftermath of September 11th and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan," said one political analyst familiar with the survey. "There's genuine uncertainty in the American public about how to engage with the Muslim world."

## Support for Outreach

Despite the mixed feelings, a significant majority of Americans — approximately 55 percent — said they supported the president's efforts to improve relations with Muslim nations through direct diplomacy and dialogue.

The poll suggests that while personal attitudes may vary, many Americans recognize the strategic importance of repairing relationships that frayed during the Bush years.

## Partisan and Generational Divides

The survey revealed notable divisions along party lines. Democrats were considerably more likely than Republicans to view Muslim countries favorably and to endorse the president's outreach strategy. Independents fell somewhere in between.

Age also emerged as a significant factor, with younger Americans expressing more positive attitudes than older generations.

## The Cairo Address

Obama's upcoming speech in Egypt is being closely watched as a potential turning point in U.S.-Muslim relations. The president has said he hopes to speak candidly about areas of tension while emphasizing shared values and common interests.

White House officials have downplayed expectations that a single speech could transform relationships overnight, framing it instead as one step in a longer process of engagement.

The president's trip will also include a stop in Saudi Arabia before the Cairo address.

*This poll was conducted among a national sample of American adults, with a sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.*

# Obama Heads to Middle East Amid High Expectations for Diplomatic Reset

**WASHINGTON** — President Barack Obama departs this week for a closely watched trip to the Middle East, seeking to reframe America's relationship with the Muslim world after years of strained ties during the Bush administration.

The visit, which includes stops in Saudi Arabia and Egypt, comes as the new president works to translate his campaign promises of renewed engagement into concrete diplomatic progress.

## A Region Watching Closely

Recent polling underscores both the opportunity and the challenge Obama faces. A survey conducted this spring found that 41 percent of respondents across several Muslim-majority nations expressed optimism that U.S. policy would improve under the new administration, though skepticism remained widespread. Domestically, Obama entered the trip with approval ratings hovering in the low 60s, giving him significant political capital as he embarks abroad.

"The expectations here are enormous, perhaps unrealistically so," said a CNN political analyst. "Obama has generated tremendous goodwill simply by not being his predecessor, but goodwill and policy are two very different things. At some point, the rhetoric has to produce results, particularly on issues like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict."

## First Stop: Saudi Arabia

Obama's itinerary begins in Riyadh, where he is scheduled to meet with King Abdullah. The Saudi stop, added to the schedule shortly before departure, signals the kingdom's strategic importance on issues ranging from oil markets to regional security and the ongoing tensions surrounding Iran's nuclear ambitions.

White House officials described the meeting as an opportunity to consult with a key ally before the president delivers his broader message to the region.

"You cannot address the major questions of the Middle East without Saudi Arabia at the table," the CNN analyst noted. "The king is a pivotal figure, and Obama clearly wants his buy-in early."

## The Centerpiece: Cairo Address

The trip's marquee event is Obama's speech in Cairo, delivered at Cairo University in a venue chosen for its symbolic weight. The address, long anticipated since Obama pledged during his campaign to speak directly to the Muslim world from a Muslim capital, is expected to touch on democracy, religious tolerance, women's rights, and the path toward peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

Egypt, the most populous Arab nation and a longtime recipient of substantial U.S. aid, offered a fitting stage. Aides emphasized that the president intended to speak candidly, acknowledging past grievances while charting a forward-looking course.

## Managing Expectations

Analysts caution that a single speech, however eloquent, will not erase decades of mistrust.

"The danger for this White House is overpromising," the CNN analyst said. "One address doesn't resolve the hardest problems in the world. But if Obama can shift the tone and open doors that were previously shut, that in itself is meaningful progress."

As Air Force One prepares to depart, the world will be listening — and watching to see whether a new chapter in American diplomacy is truly beginning.

---

*This is a fictional composition reflecting the general political context of the period.*

The survey data indicates that favorable views of the United States remain below majority thresholds in many predominantly Muslim countries. - **Regional variation**: Some nations demonstrated modest improvements, while others registered significant deterioration in public sentiment toward the United States.

- **Shared values**: The President highlighted common aspirations and the importance of partnership rather than confrontation.
- **New beginning**: His Turkey visit signaled an administration commitment to rebuilding trust through dialogue and engagement.

The survey findings, when considered alongside diplomatic initiatives like the Turkey town hall, illustrate the challenge of translating rhetorical outreach into measurable improvements in public opinion. While leadership transitions and diplomatic gestures can influence perceptions, the data suggests that deeply held views shaped by policy actions and historical events resist rapid change.

# Poll Reveals Deep Mutual Distrust Between Americans, Muslims Ahead of Obama Speech

*A CNN News Analysis*

As President Obama prepares to deliver a major address aimed at repairing relations with the Muslim world, new polling data reveals significant reservoirs of mistrust on both sides of the divide—a challenge that could complicate the administration's outreach efforts.

## The Numbers

A recently released survey highlights the depth of misunderstanding that has accumulated over years marked by war, terrorism concerns, and cultural friction. According to the poll, substantial majorities of Americans express reservations about Islam, while populations across Muslim-majority nations report deep skepticism about American intentions.

The findings suggest that whatever goodwill Obama's election generated internationally has not fully translated into trust between ordinary citizens.

## American Attitudes

Among Americans surveyed, many reported unfavorable views of Islam as a religion, with a notable segment saying they believe the faith encourages violence more than other religions do. Analysts caution these attitudes often stem from limited personal contact—polls consistently show that Americans who personally know a Muslim hold considerably more favorable views.

"There's a knowledge gap," one pollster noted. "Attitudes hardened after 9/11 and haven't fully recovered."

## Views From the Muslim World

Across Muslim-majority countries, the survey found persistent suspicion of U.S. motives, particularly regarding American military presence in the region and support for certain governments. Many respondents expressed doubt that the United States genuinely respects Islam or seeks fair treatment of Muslim nations.

However, the data also showed a measurable uptick in optimism following Obama's inauguration—a window administration officials hope to widen.

## The Stakes for Obama's Speech

The President faces the delicate task of addressing two audiences simultaneously: reassuring Muslim listeners of American respect while not appearing to apologize to domestic critics.

"He's threading a needle," said one foreign policy expert. "The speech is symbolically important, but polls remind us that words alone won't reverse years of accumulated distrust."

Whether Obama's message resonates may depend less on rhetoric and more on subsequent policy—on issues ranging from Middle East peace to the drawdown of forces in the region.
